summary: No direct evidence exists on a Kennedy general election, since he was killed in June 1968. Spring polls had Kennedy roughly level with or slightly behind Nixon, and he did well among Black voters, Catholics and working-class whites in primaries. Sources suggest he might have cut Wallace's union vote, but Wallace likely held most Southern whites.

notes:
**Scope note.** Kennedy actually died on June 5–6, so there is no direct evidence on a Kennedy general election. Nothing below breaks results out by sex, immigrant or citizenship status, or the five regions in your list. The sources I found give only a few of those cuts: Black voters, Catholics, the South, and white Southern manual workers. I flag the gaps where they matter.

## 1. Direct evidence (what scholars and pollsters say)

**Kennedy voters who lost their candidate.** I found no rigorous panel study that follows Kennedy primary voters into November. What I found is impressionistic:
- One survey text says many who had backed McCarthy and the late Kennedy refused to vote in November, others voted for Wallace, and some working-class Democrats voted for Nixon. [S19] This is a textbook summary, not measured shares.
- A reporter at Wallace rallies in Massachusetts in July 1968 wrote that many in the audiences, mostly white working-class men, had planned to vote for Robert Kennedy. [S3] That is anecdote, not a count.
- A Kennedy-era internal memo from the Indiana primary showed that Kennedy-backing voters had favorable opinions of Wallace. [S1] That is secondary-source reporting on the memo.
- The delegates did not move together either. Without any obligation, most Kennedy delegates backed Humphrey over McCarthy or fell behind George McGovern. [S2]

**Kennedy against the Republican in spring 1968.** The polls conflict, and the Gallup and Harris numbers differ.
- Gallup, April 21: Nixon 41, Kennedy 38, Wallace 10. Gallup, May 12: Nixon 42, Kennedy 32, Wallace 15. [S11] Harris, May 6: Nixon 40, Kennedy 38, Wallace 14. [S11]
- Gallup in mid-May had Nixon and Rockefeller both preferred over all three Democrats, with Kennedy doing worst of the three. [S10]
- Gallup's last poll before his death had him tied with Nixon. [S10] Pew reports the figures as Nixon 37, Kennedy 35, Wallace 17. [S14] The same poll found that adults under 30 would have picked Kennedy over Nixon, 44% to 33%. [S14]
- Earlier, in March 1966, Gallup had Kennedy beating Nixon 54% to 41%. [S10] That was before the Wallace candidacy and the 1968 shocks.
- Gallup's favorability scale in May 1968 shows no strong edge. No leading contender topped 30% "highly favorable." Kennedy's 24% put him third, behind Nixon at 28% and Humphrey at 26%. [S10]
- Humphrey, the actual nominee, polled 36–42% against Nixon at 36–39% in May and June. [S6] For comparison, Kennedy was within 2 to 10 points behind Nixon.

**Wallace.** A key interpretive claim: Louis Harris suggested a nominated Kennedy "probably would have heavily cut the Wallace vote among trade union members." [S3] The same source says in most 1968 trial heats Kennedy ran better against Wallace than any other Democrat. [S3] The source is a Century Foundation report, which is advocacy-leaning. I did not find peer-reviewed support for this.

## 2. Analogues

**Black voters.**
- Kennedy won 86% of the Black vote in Indiana and 90% in California. [S1] These are cited in a Wikipedia article that I haven't traced to its sources, so treat the figures as provisional.
- The Washington, D.C. primary, which was about two-thirds Black, went 62.5% Kennedy to 37.5% Humphrey. [S1]
- A late-May poll found that 94% of Black respondents said Kennedy had the outstanding qualities of the late President Kennedy, against 40% overall. [S1]
- A Harris survey found fewer than half viewed Humphrey as favoring a speed-up in racial progress, and only about a third viewed McCarthy that way. [S3] A Harris poll in May also ranked Kennedy first on speeding up racial progress. [S3] The source puts his share at 69%.
- In the November result Humphrey took the Black vote overwhelmingly. Of his support in the former Confederacy, a majority came from Black voters. [S6] Wikipedia also says Humphrey got 31% of the southern vote, more than two-thirds of it Black. [S22] That second figure comes from a Dissent magazine piece, which is not an academic source. I did not find Humphrey's exact Black share.

**Catholics and white ethnics.**
- Evans and Novak reported Kennedy ran 2 to 1 ahead in some Polish precincts in Indiana, while Black precincts gave him about 90%. [S3]
- A Century Foundation analysis says that statewide he did "astonishingly well" among working-class whites and Catholics. [S3] The same report cautions that revisionists draw broad conclusions from one jurisdiction. [S3]
- Actual November result: Catholics went Humphrey 59, Nixon 33, Wallace 8; Protestants went Humphrey 35, Nixon 49, Wallace 16. [S6] I did not find a comparable Kennedy projection, and this table comes from Wikipedia and needs checking against Gallup or ANES.
- The best precedent is John F. Kennedy's own 1960 coalition. The sources I have do not give the Catholic vote in 1960, so I can't offer figures.

**White Southerners.**
- Actual November result: some estimates put Humphrey below 10% of the white vote in the former Confederacy; other sources say closer to 20%. [S6] Among Southern white manual workers, Wallace won 53% (Lipset), against 22% of the middle class. [S22] The regional vote was South: Humphrey 31, Nixon 36, Wallace 33. [S6]
- Pollsters found that four out of five Wallace votes would have gone to Nixon if Wallace had not run. [S20] Nearly two-thirds of Wallace voters interviewed after they voted refused to name a second choice. [S22] The second figure is from a Dissent piece summarizing 1968 data.
- Kennedy's candidacy faced opposition from Southern Democrats, labor leaders and business. [S1] Together, these point to Wallace holding most Deep South whites under a Kennedy nomination.

**Turnout and the base.** I found no figures for turnout effects, or for men versus women, naturalized immigrants or non-citizens. The Hispanic evidence is limited to Kennedy winning large numbers of African-American, Latino and working-class white voters in California. [S9]

## 3. Named people

- **Robert Kennedy:** He refused antiwar activists' 1967 appeals to challenge Johnson, then declared on March 16, 1968, four days after McCarthy's New Hampshire showing. [S8] He spoke in Indianapolis on the King assassination days before the Indiana primary. [S1] In Indiana he reassured white voters that he was not the mouthpiece of black-power advocates or the New Left. [S5] After Nebraska he urged McCarthy supporters to back him to stop Humphrey. [S1]
- **Humphrey:** He entered on April 27, after Johnson withdrew. [S1] He had establishment backing and entered no primaries. [S4] At Kennedy's death, delegates stood at Humphrey 561, Kennedy 393, McCarthy 258. [S6] Gallup found in early June that Democratic county chairmen backed Humphrey 67%, Kennedy 19%. [S1] So Kennedy's nomination was not assured, even if he had survived.
- **Wallace:** He ran as a third-party candidate. Conservative Democrats tended to support either Humphrey or Wallace. [S2]
- **McCarthy:** He won more primary votes than Kennedy (2.91M, 38.7%, to 2.31M, 30.6% [S2]). Where the two met head-to-head, Kennedy won four contests to McCarthy's one. [S6]

## 4. Limits

- **Primary versus general electorate.** Primary electorates are small and self-selected, and Kennedy's Indiana win was a plurality. He took 42% in Indiana [S4] against Branigin's 30.7%. [S7] Kennedy also lost Oregon [S4], a homogeneous, affluent white state, and Massachusetts ended with Humphrey write-ins at 18%. [S1]
- **Wallace.** Many Wallace-curious Kennedy voters were primary voters in a race without Wallace. They may not have stayed once Kennedy faced Wallace on the ballot, since an RFK nomination was a civil-rights-forward candidacy.
- **Spring polling.** All spring Kennedy polls were before the conventions, before Chicago, and before Nixon's and Wallace's fall campaigns. The Gallup and Harris spread (a 10-point Nixon lead versus a 2-point one for the same week) is itself large. The 1966 lead is not comparable.
- **Humphrey-era shifts.** Humphrey's polling trajectory (about 28–31% in September to 40% on the eve of the election) shows how much the late campaign moved. The Kennedy-versus-Nixon numbers say nothing about this.
- **Source quality.** Some figures above come from Wikipedia, the Century Foundation or Dissent. I found no peer-reviewed or Roper Center/ANES breakdown by sex, nativity, citizenship or region. For Black, Catholic
prompt:
Scenario for the 1968 United States presidential election (election day 1968-11-05).
A reader asked: "Robert F. Kennedy survives and is the Democratic nominee in 1968.".
As modelled: Robert Kennedy is not killed in June, and he is the nominee of the party of the administration in office since 1961.
Kind of change: issue. Populations it reaches first: every voter.
Include how the same groups swung, by how much, when comparable issues or shocks hit nearby elections.

Questions to answer:
- How did voters who backed Kennedy in the 1968 primaries split in the general election when their candidate was not on the ballot?
- How did Black and Catholic voters respond to Kennedy's primary campaign compared with the eventual nominee's?
- How did Southern white Democrats who supported a third-party candidate view a Kennedy nomination?
- What did polls in spring 1968 show for Kennedy against the Republican candidate?

Groups the simulation distinguishes: men and women; native-born white, naturalized immigrant, non-citizen immigrant and Black adults; the Northeast, Midwest, South (the eleven former Confederate states), border states and West. Evidence by these groups is most useful.
